Dear Kunal,

You asked how I decided about Pune, so here's the honest answer: I haven't, not fully.

The offer there is better. More money, better projects. But Maa's knee is getting worse, and Baba won't say it but he's scared of managing alone. If I stay in Indore, I take a smaller job but I'm home for dinner.

I made a list. Pune has more boxes ticked. But the list doesn't know how I'll feel missing Maa's surgery.

Maa told me not to stay for them. Baba said nothing, which is his way of saying something.

I've asked Pune if I could start in three months instead. If they say yes, I can see Maa through the surgery first. If not, I'll choose then, knowing I tried.

Write back. What would you do?

Hemant

The acceptance email came at 2 a.m., and I read it standing in the hallway so I wouldn't wake Amma. A master's place in Bengaluru, with a stipend that would barely cover rent.

Two days earlier, the bank in Madurai had offered me a clerk's job. Permanent. Ten minutes from home.

Amma said, "Take the bank job, kanna. Your sister's wedding is next year." Sarita Chithi said the opposite: "She'll regret it forever if she doesn't go." Everyone had an opinion, and nobody knew what the course would lead to, including me.

So I made two columns on the back of a calendar. Not pros and cons, but "what I know" and "what I'm guessing". The guessing column was much longer.

In the end I asked the bank if I could defer for a year. They said no. I took Bengaluru anyway, and told Amma I would send part of the stipend home. I'm Kalyani, and I still don't know if I chose right. I only know I chose, instead of letting the loudest voice choose for me.

Mentor's note, placement cell.

Tanvir met me today about the offer from the Dubai office. He brought two sheets of paper: one with the salary and visa details, the other with his parents' concerns, written in his own words. I found that unusual and thoughtful.

His father has asked him to stay in Lucknow for two years, because the family is planning his elder sister's move abroad after her marriage. His mother wants him to go. Tanvir said, "Whichever I pick, someone in the house feels let down."

He did not know yet whether the Dubai role had a path to promotion, or what the rent would be. I suggested he email the recruiter three specific questions before deciding, and that he ask his parents to talk it through together rather than one at a time. He looked relieved to have a next step.

I will see him again after he hears back. I did not tell him which to choose.

— Thomas Varghese

Ammi and Abba met Rehana's family today. Everyone was sweet, there were too many samosas, and on the way home Abba said, "Beta, they are good people. Think about it."

The thing is, I did like talking to her. Rehana wants to do her PhD in Hyderabad. I have an offer in Pune starting in August. We are both twenty-two. If we say yes now, one of us moves, or we spend two years on trains.

In their small town in Gujarat, Swati's parents had found a proposal: Darshan, an engineer in Surat. Families had met. Everyone was smiling. Swati felt the decision rushing at her like a train.
She asked to meet Darshan alone, for an hour, at the town's only café. Her mother raised her eyebrows but agreed.
Swati came with questions written on her phone: where they'd live, whether she could keep teaching, how he felt about her parents visiting, how he handled arguments. Darshan was surprised, then laughed. "Can I ask mine too?" He asked about money habits and whether she wanted children soon.
They didn't agree on everything. He wanted to stay in Surat; she hoped for somewhere near her school.
Walking home, Swati told her mother, "I'm not saying no. I need two more meetings." Her mother, after a pause, said, "That's fair."

Aiko got the call on a Tuesday: a design job in Tokyo, the kind she'd dreamed of since university. Her partner, Zanele, had just started a teaching post in Cape Town, and they'd been together two years.
They sat on the floor of their flat with two lists. Aiko's: career, being closer to her ageing parents. Zanele's: a job she'd fought for, her sister's new baby.
"What do we actually know?" Zanele asked. The salary. The flight time. That Aiko's contract had a one-year review.
"What don't we know?" Whether long distance would work. Whether Zanele could find teaching work in Tokyo. Whether either of them would regret it.
Aiko's parents said, "Come home." Zanele's sister said, "Don't lose each other."
They decided to try one year apart, with visits every three months, and a fixed date to decide again. Neither was sure. Both felt heard.

qa.q: How did Aiko and Zanele feel about their decision?
qa.a: Neither was sure, but both felt heard, which made the uncertainty easier to carry.

qa.a: They listed each person's needs, separated what they knew from what they didn't, heard family, and set a trial year with a review date.
